content: Casting is a manufacturing process where a liquid material is poured into a mold that contains a hollow cavity in the desired shape. The material is then allowed to solidify, after which the solidified casting is removed from the mold. This process is commonly used for forming hot liquid metals or materials that set at room temperature, such as epoxies, concrete, plaster, and clay. Casting is particularly advantageous for creating complex shapes that would be difficult or expensive to produce using other methods. The process has been in use for over 6,000 years, with the oldest known casting being a copper frog from 3200 BC. Casting methods are broadly categorized into expendable mold casting and non-expendable mold casting. Expendable Mold Casting Expendable mold casting involves the use of temporary molds that are destroyed after a single use. Examples include sand, plastic, shell, plaster, and investment (lost-wax) moldings. Waste Molding of Plaster In this method, a durable plaster mold is created as an intermediate step, often for producing bronze sculptures or as a guide for stone carving. Plaster molds are more durable than clay originals, which must remain moist to prevent cracking. This allows the expensive processes of bronze casting or stone carving to be deferred until a suitable patron is found. A thin plaster mold, reinforced with materials like sisal or burlap, is cast over the original clay. Once cured, the mold is removed, destroying the clay but preserving its details. This mold can then be used to cast a single plaster positive, which can be refined, painted, or waxed to resemble a finished bronze piece. Sand Casting Sand casting is one of the oldest and simplest casting methods, allowing for the production of small to large parts at a relatively low cost. It is versatile, accommodating a wide range of sizes, from small hand-held items to large train beds. Sand molds can be made using green sand (moist sand bonded with clay) or dry sand (bonded with chemical binders or oils). Green sand molds have no weight limit, while dry sand molds can handle parts weighing up to 2,700 kg. Sand casting is ideal for high-output production, with rates of 1-20 pieces per hour per mold. The sand used in this process can often be recycled, making it cost-effective and sustainable. Plaster Casting (of Metals) Plaster casting is similar to sand casting but uses plaster instead of sand. The plaster mixture typically consists of 70-80% gypsum, 20-30% strengtheners, and water. This method is suitable for producing parts with high surface resolution and fine tolerances, such as lock components, gears, valves, and ornaments. However, the quality of the mold depends on factors like the consistency of the plaster mixture, pouring techniques, and curing methods. Plaster molds are not reusable and are limited to non-ferrous metals like aluminum, zinc, and copper alloys, as gypsum reacts with iron and cannot withstand temperatures above 1,200°C. Before casting, the pattern is coated with a parting compound to prevent sticking, and the plaster is dried and preheated before molten metal is poured. Casting of Plaster, Concrete, or Plastic Resin Plaster, concrete, and plastic resin can also be cast using single-use or reusable molds. These materials are less visually appealing than marble and are often painted to mimic metal or stone. Concrete is particularly suitable for outdoor sculptures, fountains, or seating. Plastic resins, such as epoxy or polyester, can be mixed with powdered stone to simulate high-quality marble, often used for washstands and shower stalls. Shell Molding Shell molding uses a mixture of sand and resin to create molds with high precision. The process involves heating a metal pattern, inverting it into a sand-resin mixture, and curing the shell. This method is ideal for small, intricate parts like gear housings and cylinder heads. Shell molding allows for the production of 5-50 pieces per hour per mold and is highly automated, reducing labor costs. Investment Casting Investment casting, also known as lost-wax casting, is an ancient technique that produces high-quality components with intricate details. Wax patterns are surrounded by a refractory material to create the mold. The wax is melted away, leaving a cavity for molten metal. This process is suitable for small to medium-sized parts and can produce components with minimal rework. While more expensive than other methods, investment casting is highly accurate and versatile, capable of producing parts from various metals and alloys. Non-Expendable Mold Casting Non-expendable mold casting uses molds that can be reused multiple times, reducing the need for mold reformation. This category includes permanent mold casting, die casting, centrifugal casting, and continuous casting. Permanent Mold Casting Permanent mold casting involves steel molds coated with a refractory material to facilitate part removal and extend mold life. This method is typically used for non-ferrous metals like aluminum, magnesium, and copper alloys. Permanent molds produce parts with higher tensile strength and elongation compared to sand casting. The process is highly automated and efficient, with production rates of 5-50 pieces per hour per mold. It is commonly used for non-ferrous metals like zinc, copper, and aluminum alloys. Die casting is ideal for producing large quantities of small to medium-sized parts. This method is suitable for producing parts with fine details, such as jewelry, or large industrial components like railway wheels. The process can produce 30-50 pieces per hour per mold and is often used in conjunction with the lost-wax technique. Continuous Casting Continuous casting is designed for the high-volume production of metal sections with a constant cross-section. Molten metal is poured into a water-cooled mold, forming a solidified skin while the center remains liquid. The strand is gradually solidified as it passes through rollers and water sprays. This method is cost-effective and produces high-quality products, commonly used for metals like steel, copper, and aluminum. Cooling Rate The cooling rate of a casting significantly impacts its microstructure and quality. Molding materials transfer heat at different rates, influencing how the metal solidifies. Foundry engineers carefully plan the cooling process to avoid defects like gas or shrinkage porosities. Shrinkage All castings shrink as they cool due to the increased density of solid metal compared to liquid metal. Shrinkage occurs during both solidification and cooling to room temperature. To compensate, risers are used to supply additional material during solidification, and patterns are made oversized using contraction rulers.
